activities.anchor: The storage hierarchy is worth learning as a speed ladder
activities.caption: line up the speed ladder, fastest first
activities.name: ictLadderOrder

config.prompt: The storage hierarchy — order it, fastest and smallest first:
items: Hard disk — slower, cheap per gigabyte, permanent
config.why: Each step down buys capacity with latency — which is why opening an app 'loads it into RAM': dragging the program up the ladder so the CPU can fetch from it at full speed.

activities.caption: file each program under its family
activities.name: ictSoftwareBuckets

config.prompt: Who is each program for? File it:

items.label: databases, video and graphics editing, CAD, web browsers

config.why: The test that separates them: could this program exist without a user? A spreadsheet exists for the user; a compiler exists for the machine.

activities.anchor: schedule which program gets the CPU
activities.caption: find the faulty line — who touches the metal
activities.name: ictOsSpot

config.prompt: One line of this startup-and-services summary is wrong — click it:
lines: The OS starts first, from ROM's bootstrap.
It loads drivers for the hardware present.
Applications then launch and request services through the OS.
Applications touch the hardware directly, for speed.
That indirection is why the same application runs on many different machines.
config.correction: Applications go through the OS — memory allocation, file access, screen drawing, networking — rather than touching the hardware directly.
config.why: Applications talk to the OS's stable interface, not to the metal — which is why the same application runs on many different machines.

config.prompt: OS types matched to the work — pair them:

pairs.right: jobs with no interaction at all — a payroll run works through the night
each open task gets a tiny slice of CPU time — a quantum — then switches
work spread across many interconnected machines, each with its own memory and CPU
the older specialists that first let personal computers share files and printers

config.why: Your laptop descends from the Linux and Unix family — done fast enough, dozens of programs appear to run at once.

activities.anchor: The professional skill the section tests is matching type to task
activities.caption: match the machine to the job
activities.name: ictMachineBranch

config.root: Four briefs land on your desk. Match each to its machine — and say what you traded away.

start.text: The types are one machine at different points of a decades-long shrink.

choices.label: A film editor cutting 4K footage all day
choices.feedback: Sustained power, cheap expandability, the best cooling — portability is the trade.

choices.label: A student writing essays between class and home
choices.feedback: The battery-powered clamshell — paying in price, repair difficulty and thermal limits.

choices.label: A washing machine's cycle controller
choices.feedback: The same idea frozen into one fixed program in ROM — a small, single-program computer is still a computer.

choices.label: Mainframe-style workloads for a bank
choices.feedback: The same fetch–decode–execute cycle, scaled up in racks.

desktop.text: The desktop trades portability for everything else.

laptop.text: Same architecture, folded into a clamshell.

embedded.text: Instant-on, single-purpose — and still a computer by every definition in this lesson.

server.text: Racks of the same cycle — scale, not novelty.

config.why: Instant-on, always-connected, sensor-rich tablets and phones push furthest into portability — and pay in screen size, input precision and upgradeability.

config.prompt: Intel's 4004 (1971) carried about 2,300 transistors; the 2022 Apple M1 Ultra carries about 114 billion. Roughly how many times more is that?
config.why: 2,300 → 114 billion is roughly fifty million times — and a straight line on a log scale means exponential growth: Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that component counts double roughly every two years.
config.context: Every equal vertical step on the lesson's plot is a tenfold jump — the distance from the 1993 Pentium to the 2000 Pentium 4 alone is roughly thirteen times.
